passage: In the first week of the polytechnic course, I was the only one who put a hand up and asked what "earthing" actually meant. I'm Indu, by the way, and I remember the lab going silent. Someone at the back muttered, "Didn't you do Class 10?" My face burned. But Mr Pillai drew a stick figure touching a wire, explained it slowly, and for the first time it clicked. Ganga, on the stool beside me, had nodded all through that lecture. That night she messaged me: "Can you explain earthing? I didn't get it either." Looking back, that question cost me thirty seconds of embarrassment. By the practical exam I had asked maybe forty more like it. Ganga later told me she spent the term copying my notes and hoping nobody noticed the gaps. I don't think I was cleverer. I was just less busy pretending.

qa.q: What did Indu ask in the first week of the course?
qa.a: Indu asked what "earthing" actually meant.

qa.q: How did Indu feel right after someone muttered about Class 10?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed, with a burning face, but kept listening and soon felt the relief of the idea finally clicking.

qa.q: What could Ganga have tried during that lecture instead of nodding?
qa.a: She could have raised her hand too, or caught Mr Pillai after class, rather than hoping nobody noticed the gaps.

qa.q: How might Ganga look back on that term?
qa.a: Ganga might feel some regret that hiding her confusion left her copying notes, and some gratitude that Indu's questions helped her as well.

grounding: Shows a student who asks a basic question without shame learning faster than a classmate who nods and hides confusion.

passage:
In the office pantry, Sabina sighed over her coffee. "Honestly, I'm so bad at presentations. The client only asked for my deck in the follow-up because they felt sorry for me."
"No way," said Nikhil. "It was brilliant!"
"Stop, it was nothing. Just three all-nighters." Sabina glanced sideways. "Right, Sharmila? Nothing special?"
Sharmila stirred her tea. "The data slide was really strong. The ending ran a bit long."
Sabina's smile flickered. "Oh. Yeah. Totally." She picked up her mug and left.
Nikhil leaned in. "Did she want us to argue with her?"
"I think she wanted us to say it was amazing," Sharmila said quietly, "without having to say it herself."
"Why not just say she's proud of it?"
Sharmila rinsed her cup. "Maybe fishing feels safer than asking."

qa.q: What did Sabina say the client asked for in the follow-up?
qa.a: She said the client asked for her deck in the follow-up.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she gave Sabina balanced feedback instead of praise?
qa.a: She seemed a little uncomfortable with the fishing for compliments and chose to be kind but honest, naming the strong data slide and the long ending.

qa.q: What could Sabina say the next time she is proud of her work?
qa.a: She could say, "I worked hard on this and I'm pleased with it. Any feedback?", which invites real praise and real notes without pretending.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Sharmila's reply was balanced?
qa.a: She probably felt deflated and a bit exposed, since her smile flickered when the praise she was fishing for did not come.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone call their own work nothing while fishing for praise, and others quietly seeing through it.

passage:
Saturday
Jomon's diary. Devika broke my ship model today. The one with the matchstick mast that took me two weeks. I found it in pieces behind the sofa and shouted so loud that Amma came running. I called Devika a destroyer and said I hate her. She didn't even cry. She just hid under the dining table.
After dinner I was still angry. But then I remembered she was hiding, not laughing. When I break something at Ammachi's house I hide too, because I'm scared, not because I wanted it broken. Maybe she was scared of me.
I told her I'm not angry anymore. That was only half true. The mast is still broken.

qa.q: How long did the ship model take Jomon to make?
qa.a: It took two weeks.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling after dinner?
qa.a: Jomon still felt angry about the ship but also started to feel sorry, realising Devika had hidden because she was scared, not mean.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Devika do together about the broken mast?
qa.a: They could glue the mast together, and Jomon could calmly ask what happened, so Devika learns she can own up without hiding 🙂

qa.q: Why might Devika have hidden under the dining table?
qa.a: She was probably frightened by the shouting and by what she had done, so hiding felt safer than explaining.

grounding: Shows a child working out that a younger sibling who broke a toy was scared rather than mean, while the anger only partly fades.

passage:
Friday. "You never trust me!" Noor shouted, and slammed her door. Abbu's voice came through it: "The party ends at eleven, and that flyover road has no lights—" She didn't hear the rest. All she heard was no. Divyansh's whole class would be there, and she would be the only one missing.
Sunday. Noor woke early and found Abbu asleep in his chair by the window, still in his office shirt, his phone on his chest. Ammi said quietly, "He waited up to see if you'd go anyway."
Tuesday. Noor sat beside him on the balcony. "You weren't saying no to me. You were scared of the road." Abbu let out a long breath. "Very scared." They agreed: next time, he would drive her and pick her up by ten-thirty.

qa.q: What time did Divyansh's party end?
qa.a: The party ended at eleven.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling on Friday night?
qa.a: Noor felt angry and hurt, sure that Abbu did not trust her, so she heard only the no.

qa.q: What could Noor try the next time a quarrel heats up?
qa.a: She could say she needs a break and come back to it the next day, when she can hear the reasons as well as the no.

qa.q: How did Abbu see the party request?
qa.a: He was afraid of Noor travelling home late on the dark flyover road, so his no came from fear, not distrust.

grounding: Shows a teenager who can see only her own side while quarrelling with her father, and who understands his fear once she has calmed down.

passage: Last winter, when my name was missing from the district basketball list, I decided my life was basically finished. I'm Rukmini, and I was very dramatic about it. Everyone gave advice. "Try next year." "Focus on studies." I stopped hearing any of it. Then one night Gopika Paati, who never talks about the past, sat on the edge of my bed and told me about the year she turned nineteen. The mill closed, and she lost the only job in the family. She cried for a week, then learned typing on a borrowed machine, and two years later she was the fastest typist at the collector's office. "That week felt like forever," she said. "Now it's one line in a long story." She didn't tell me what to do. But I started counting my life in decades instead of weeks. I made the list this October.

qa.q: What did Gopika Paati learn after she lost her mill job?
qa.a: She learned typing on a borrowed machine.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when the name was missing from the list?
qa.a: Rukmini felt crushed and hopeless, deciding life was basically finished and no longer hearing anyone's advice.

qa.q: Why did Paati's story help more than the advice?
qa.a: It showed a real hard week inside a long life, so Rukmini could feel the longer timeline instead of just being told to wait.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gopika Paati to share that memory?
qa.a: Since she never talks about the past, it may have felt tender to reopen, and also warm to see her hard week help Rukmini.

grounding: Shows a grandparent's story of hardship and recovery giving a teenager a longer timeline for a sports setback than advice alone could.

passage:
Hostel warden's log, Block C, Wednesday, 11 pm.
Chetan came to the office pale, laptop in hand. His final-year project drive had failed two days before submission. He kept saying, "It's over, everything's over." His roommate Shankar came with him. I made tea and let him talk. After a while I asked what I ask everyone in that chair: "A year from now, who will remember this, and how much?" He went quiet, then counted on his fingers: his guide, himself, maybe his parents. "The guide will remember whether I told him early," he said. That seemed to steady him. He agreed to email the guide that night and ask about an extension. Shankar offered his old laptop and the printed drafts. I checked in at 8 am. The email had gone, and the guide had replied.

qa.q: How many days before submission did Chetan's drive fail?
qa.a: It failed two days before submission.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he arrived at the office?
qa.a: He felt panicked and hopeless, pale and repeating that everything was over.

qa.q: Which question helped Chetan, and why?
qa.a: Asking who would remember this in a year, and how much, shrank the disaster to a few people and pointed him to one step: telling his guide early.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt standing beside Chetan that night?
qa.a: Shankar was probably worried for his roommate and glad to be useful, offering his old laptop and the printed drafts.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing a project disaster zooming out to a year ahead, which calms the panic without pretending the loss is small.

passage:
September. At the inter-college debate, Vikas took apart the other team's case in four minutes flat, and the hall roared. Sangeeta, who taught his philosophy section, clapped too, though she noticed he had argued the side he'd told her last week he didn't believe.
November. Passing the attendance office, she heard Vikas, quick and charming, talking the clerk into overlooking three weeks of missed labs. He had joined four clubs, quit his internship after a quarrel with his manager, and looked as if he hadn't slept.
February. He stood at her desk holding his results. "Sixty-one percent. I'm sharper than half that class." Sangeeta nodded. "You are. What were you trying to win this year?" He opened his mouth, then closed it.

qa.q: How long did Vikas take to take apart the other team's case?
qa.a: He took four minutes flat.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she clapped in September?
qa.a: She was impressed but also uneasy, because he had argued a side he had told her he didn't believe.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta's question help Vikas more than praise or a lecture?
qa.a: It makes him weigh what was worth pursuing this year and at what cost, which his quick arguing had skipped.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas when he cannot answer her question?
qa.a: He probably feels stung and confused, since being sharp has always been enough and, for once, it is not.

grounding: Shows a teacher watching a brilliant student win every argument while his choices go badly, separating cleverness from wisdom.

passage: I'm Afreen, and for a month I watched my older sister Zeenat collect opinions like stamps. She called Khala, who once left Lucknow to teach in a mountain village. She met a man from her old college who had done the same two-year teaching fellowship and quit after one. She even asked our neighbour, who has never left the colony, and actually listened. Every night she wrote in a green notebook. I couldn't tell if she was scared or excited; maybe both. The man's story seemed to shake her, because she went quiet for two days. Then on Sunday she showed Ammi a page with three lines: "I want to teach. I want to be nearer home by thirty. Two years fits." She signed the form that evening. Nobody had told her to.

qa.q: Where did Khala once go to teach?
qa.a: She once left Lucknow to teach in a mountain village.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been feeling after hearing from the man who quit?
qa.a: She may have felt shaken and unsure, since she went quiet for two days after hearing his story.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's way of deciding get right?
qa.a: She asked people with different experiences, including someone who quit, then checked their views against her own three lines before deciding herself.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the page Zeenat showed her?
qa.a: Ammi may feel reassured that the choice was thought through and tied to being nearer home by thirty, even if two years away will be hard.

grounding: Shows a young adult consulting people who lived through a similar choice, then weighing their views against her own values and deciding herself.

passage: The night train was hot and crowded, and the baby across the aisle, Jatin, had been crying since Kota. He kept reaching for Rekha's tin bird. "Rekha, let him hold it for a little while," Mummy said. Rekha squeezed the bird. "It's mine." "Just till he sleeps. Please, beta." Rekha held it out slowly, her fingers opening one at a time. Jatin stopped crying at once. Rekha did not. She pushed her face into Mummy's dupatta and peeked at the bird over her arm the whole time, counting its wings.

qa.q: What toy did Rekha give to Jatin?
qa.a: She gave him her tin bird.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after handing over the bird?
qa.a: She felt sad and anxious about her toy 🥺, hiding her face in Mummy's dupatta and watching the bird the whole time.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to help Rekha with this kind of sharing?
qa.a: Mummy could thank Rekha, say that it was hard, and make sure the bird comes back when Jatin sleeps, so sharing feels safe next time.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha had chosen to share without being asked?
qa.a: Giving the bird would have felt like her own kind choice, so she might feel warm about it instead of only feeling the loss.

grounding: Shows a young child handing over a toy on a crowded train after a parent's urging while still feeling the loss keenly.

passage: Kamal, you asked why I always pack an extra roti. When I was nine, at the municipal school near the mill, there was a boy called Bhola who never opened a tiffin. One day his stomach growled so loudly the whole row laughed. At lunch I didn't ask anyone. I tore my paratha in half, put it on his slate, and went back to my place. He didn't say thank you. He just ate, very fast. I walked home that day feeling taller, warm right through, though I was hungry by evening. Nobody told me to do it again, but I did, most days, till the term ended. After that, your Nilesh Dadu was "the one who shares" in his own head. Sixty years later, I still am.

qa.q: What did Nilesh put on Bhola's slate?
qa.a: He put half of his paratha on it.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel walking home that day?
qa.a: He felt warm right through and proud, "taller", even though he was hungry by evening 😊

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's choice at lunch matter so much, in the story?
qa.a: No one told him to share, so the choice was his own, and repeating it made him see himself as someone who shares.

qa.q: How might Bhola have felt when the paratha appeared on his slate?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and a little embarrassed after the laughing, which could be why he ate fast without saying thank you.

grounding: Shows a child freely giving half his lunch to a hungry classmate and growing a lasting sense of himself as generous.
